title: Pasta with Tomato Sauce and Seafood

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with tomato sauce and seafood is an Italian-inspired dish where al dente pasta is tossed with a fragrant sauce made from ripe tomatoes, olive oil, garlic, and a mix of fresh seafood such as shrimp, mussels, and calamari. The dish provides protein, healthy fats, and vitamins, delivering a bright sea‑flavored taste balanced by the acidity of tomatoes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Italian tomato sauce often uses San Marzano tomatoes, known for their high sugar content.
Seafood is usually added at the end of cooking to preserve its tenderness and flavor.
Al dente pasta has a lower glycemic index than overcooked pasta.
The dish is popular in Mediterranean coastal regions where fresh seafood is available year‑round.
Tomatoes boost iron absorption from seafood thanks to their vitamin C content.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Shrimp, mussels, and calamari provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Mussels and calamari are rich in omega‑3s, which support heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Vitamin C and lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes supply vitamin C and lycopene, powerful antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals (iron, zinc, selenium)
items.content: Seafood delivers iron, zinc, and selenium, nutrients important for immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Prepared with olive oil, the dish contains mainly monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels, or calamari.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the sauce uses canned tomato paste or broth, sodium levels can be high; choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Potential toxins in shellfish
items.content: Mussels can accumulate biotoxins in polluted waters; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Overcooked pasta
items.content: Overcooking pasta reduces texture and raises its glycemic index, which may be undesirable for blood‑sugar control.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossing it with the sauce and seafood just before plating. Garnish with fresh basil, grated Parmesan, or a pinch of red pepper flakes for extra heat. The dish is eaten with a fork and spoon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Cool the dish completely before sealing. Keep seafood separate from the pasta if possible to prevent cross‑contamination.
